Giovanni Diodati
jō-van'nē dyō-dah'tē
n. (Giovanni Diodati, 1576–1649, Genevan divine of Lucchese exile stock, translator of the Italian Bible)
Italian Giovanni, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Diodati, given of God, from Latin Deodatus.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Giovanni Diodati was born at Geneva to a merchant house that had fled Lucca for the faith. He was made professor of Hebrew at nineteen, succeeded Theodore Beza in the chair of theology in 1609, and served the Genevan church for half a century. In 1607 he published the Italian Bible that bears his name, translated from the Hebrew and Greek and furnished with annotations, revised in 1641 with the metrical psalms; it remains the Bible of Italian Protestantism to this day. He made a French version as well, and the English Parliament had his notes translated in 1643, so that English Puritans read Diodati on their own Bibles. He was one of the delegates to the Synod of Dort and stood with the strictest party there against the Remonstrants. His life answers a question the Italian Reformation otherwise leaves open: what the exiles' children did with their fathers' losses. They printed the Scriptures in the tongue their fathers had been driven out of. “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an annotation as a remark or note on a text, and to expound as to explain or lay open the sense.

expand to see more

ANNOTA'TION, n. A remark, note or commentary on some passage of a book, intended to illustrate its meaning.

EXPOUND', v. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.

DIS'TINCTLY, adv. Not confusedly; plainly; clearly; with clear and distinct utterance.

SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.

Key Scripture

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Act 8:30 — "And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?"

1Co 14:9 — "So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air."

2Ti 3:15 — "And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus."

Modern Corruption

The exiles' son who gave Italy its Protestant Bible.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a modern one about translation itself: that a version carrying doctrinal notes is by that fact a partisan Bible, while a bare text is neutral. Diodati's notes are confessedly Reformed, and he said so on the title page; the pretence of neutrality belongs to versions that smuggle their theology into the rendering instead of printing it in the margin where a reader can weigh it.

The principle to recover is that translation and exposition are two offices and both are owed to the people. Ezra's Levites did not stop at reading — they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — and Philip's question to the eunuch assumes that a man may have the text and still want the sense: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew parash (H6567), to make distinct, declare; Greek ginosko (G1097), to know.

Hebrew parash (H6567) — to separate, make distinct, declare; Nehemiah 8:8.

Hebrew sekel (H7922) — understanding, sense, discretion; Nehemiah 8:8.

Greek anaginosko (G314) — to read, to know again; Acts 8:30.

Greek eusemos (G2154) — well-marked, easy to understand; 1 Corinthians 14:9.

Greek sophizo (G4679) — to make wise, instruct; 2 Timothy 3:15.

Usage

"“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — text and annotations together."

"“Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30) — the question a translator serves."

"“from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15) — what an Italian household gained in 1607."
